Agents Hunting Agents · Investigation walkthrough
SEV-1 · ACTIVE INCIDENT
02
01
Identify the assets
You can’t investigate what you can’t see. Define what was touched — and what it’s worth — before you chase a single log.
What’s in scope?
Hosts, user and service accounts, cloud tenants, and AI agents tied to the alert.
What does it do?
Business function, owner, and data sensitivity — credentials, PII, CUI.
How is it connected?
Trust paths an attacker could follow: who talks to whom, and with what permissions.
Lab artifacts → asset inventories · network maps · architecture diagrams
Step 1 · Scope & collect
SEV-1 · ACTIVE INCIDENT
03
02
Gather logs and evidence
Pull every source that touched the in-scope assets — then preserve it before it rolls over.
Preserve → read-only copies · SHA-256 hashes · chain of custody · retention windows
Zeek
DNS, HTTP, Conn and SSL logs
Internal DNS
Who resolved what, and when
Host EDR · JSONL
Process, file and network events
Firewall + NetFlow
Allowed, denied and volume of flows
App audit trails
Logins, API calls, config changes
Context
Support tickets and briefings
HINT · Check the clock
Timestamps may be in server-local time, or already in UTC. Note each source’s time zone as you collect it.
Step 2 · Scope & collect
SEV-1 · ACTIVE INCIDENT
04
03
Put the activity in order
Different sources, different clocks. Convert every timestamp to UTC, then merge into one sorted stream.
Lab tool → tools/timeline.py merges multi-format logs with time-zone-aware alignment
BEFORE · RAW, MIXED CLOCKS
1773454267.2 conn 10.0.4.17 → 203.0.113.50:443
Mar 13 21:11:09 fw ALLOW 10.0.4.17 → 203.0.113.50
2026-03-14T02:11:05Z dns q=cdn-upd4te.example.com
AFTER · UTC, SORTED
02:11:05Z dns q=cdn-upd4te.example.com
02:11:07Z conn 10.0.4.17 → 203.0.113.50:443
02:11:09Z fw ALLOW 10.0.4.17 → 203.0.113.50
HINT · Server time or UTC?
The firewall line has no zone — it’s server-local (UTC−5). Read naively, it lands five hours early.

Correlate to known events
Pivot on shared keys to connect the dots across sources, then match what you find to known adversary behavior.
Pivot keys
IP address
hostname
user / token
domain
process + hash
time window
What you observed
Known event it matches
Lookup of a look-alike domain, then steady beacons
Threat-intel IOC · ATT&CK T1071 Application Layer Protocol
Agent runtime spawns an encoded PowerShell
ATT&CK T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter
Service token used from a new IP
Credential-exposure alert · ATT&CK T1078 Valid Accounts

HINT · Label every timestamp
Write the zone on every time in the report (02:11Z, not 02:11). A reader in another office will convert an unlabeled time from server-local — and get it wrong.
Step 5 · Analyze
SEV-1 · ACTIVE INCIDENT
07
From analysis to action
The timeline is the story. Now get it to the people who must act.
06
Present findings
Same facts, different questions. Lead with impact, back every claim with evidence, and mark what is confirmed versus suspected.
Watch the clock → e.g., DoD contractors report cyber incidents within 72 hours (DFARS 252.204-7012)
Leadership
Business impact, risk, and the decisions needed now. Plain language, one page.
IT & engineering
Indicators, affected systems, containment and fix steps.
Legal & compliance
Data involved, notification duties, evidence handling.
Authorities & partners
Law enforcement, regulators, CISA or contracting officers — as law and policy require.
Step 6 · Communicate
SEV-1 · CONTAINED · REPORTING
09
07
Root cause & report
File what your organization’s policy requires — its format, approvers and deadlines.
Ask “why?” until it’s fixable
Agent ran PowerShell → token was stolen
Token stolen → it sat in a public repo
In a public repo → no secret scanning in CI
Report outline
1 · Executive summary
2 · Scope & affected assets
3 · Timeline (UTC)
4 · Root cause
5 · Impact
6 · Response & containment
7 · Remediation & owners
8 · Lessons learned
Attach the evidence: hashes, log excerpts and chain-of-custody records
